title: What the Channel Feeds
logline: A family's paddy season is held up by supports that each arrive on their own schedule and from other people's hands, and only if they all keep arriving does any of it become a meal.
human_question: How many things have to keep arriving, and keep on arriving, before one family can eat what they grew?

situation.what_happens: A farming household sows a season of paddy on a small plot fed by a shared irrigation reservoir. The water is not theirs to take when they want it: a meeting of cultivators sets when the sluice opens and in which order the fields are served, and their turn comes when it comes. Over the following months the crop is carried by supports that arrive separately and differently — the seed's own strength at the start, then released water, borrowed hands, fertiliser and whatever the weather does — and the family's work is largely the work of keeping each of them coming. At the end there is a harvest, or a thin one, and a first cooked meal of the new rice.
situation.who_is_involved: The household that farms the plot, including whoever does the daily watching of the field; the other cultivators who draw on the same water and sit in the same meeting; whoever keeps the order of turns and settles disagreements about it; the neighbours and hired hands who come for transplanting and harvest; and, at the far end, whoever eats the rice, who need not be anyone who grew it.
situation.what_is_at_stake: A year of income and a year of food for the household, and their standing with the same neighbours they will need again next season. Each support helps in its own way and cannot be substituted: water late at the wrong week is not made good by more fertiliser, and a strong seed cannot carry a crop that is not watered.
situation.how_it_unfolds: Such a season begins with a decision that is not the family's own, tightens through the weeks when the crop needs a support that has not yet come, and ends either in a harvest, in a poor one, or in a crop given up on partway. Whether the film reaches a first meal of new rice, and what mood that meal is eaten in, is decided by the rain, the water order, the labour available and the price at the end, not by the film.

concept_merge.why_together: C075 supplies the sustaining cause, and its source's own picture is agricultural: a seed is what starts a rice plant, but water and fertiliser are what keep it growing for months, so what begins a thing and what keeps it going are different jobs. C082 supplies the insistence that nothing arises from a single condition and that each support helps by its own particular power — the source's own image is a match head and the side of the box, which would not both be needed if they helped in the same way. C078 supplies the two lengths at which any of this can be told: the brief account and the detailed one. A shared-water paddy season is where these three meet without being arranged, because the supports are separately owned, separately timed and individually nameable.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: Put together, they stop 'many things had to come together' from becoming a warm slogan. The film can name each support, say what job it does and show that no other support can do that job instead; and it can set the one-line answer a farmer gives for the season against the long chain the same film has just followed, without either answer being wrong.

concept_links.why: The nutriment section's own simile is a rice seedling: the seed's strength is chief for the plant to begin, while water and fertiliser are chief for it to grow and last. A paddy season carries that distinction between what starts something and what sustains it without any need to state it.

Both sources say nothing arises from a single condition and that different conditions help in different ways; the released water, the borrowed labour, the seed and the weather are separate, nameable supports with different powers, not a general sense that everything is connected.

The sources teach cause and effect at different lengths and hold that the brief account and the detailed account are both true and both needed; a farmer's one line about the season and the long chain behind it are the same relation at two distances.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: One meal needs many different supports at once, and they do not all do the same job: a seed starts the rice plant, while water, fertiliser and other hands are what keep it going for months. The short answer a family gives for how the season went and the long chain behind it are both true.
what_must_be_real: The household's actual water-sharing arrangement and their actual place in the turn order, their real obligations and debts to the people who help them, and the season's real outcome including a poor one. No support may be arranged, hurried or supplied so that a chain looks complete.
position_hint: opening candidate: the group's plainest and slowest statement of its question, where supports can be counted one at a time before any of the harder ideas are asked for. An Object 9 acquisition is possible here only if something that exists because of this whole chain is genuinely given, never arranged for the film.
risks: Pastoral cliche: rural hardship photographed as something beautiful.
Treating the household as an illustration of a doctrine rather than people with debts, rain and prices.
Filming a disagreement over water as manufactured drama.
Letting 'many supports' soften into 'everything is connected', which both sources explicitly refuse.
The Pradeepika elsewhere links merit in a past life to present wealth or hardship; nothing in the film may present this household's circumstances that way.
drop_if: No household is willing to be followed through a whole season, including a disappointing one.
No real decision about the water order occurs while filming.
The chain can only be shown by arranging or accelerating parts of it.

connections.note: Both are openings built on something that exists only because many separate supports each did their own part.
The held idea about a shared meal picks up the same food at the point where it stops being a supply chain and becomes a memory people take up differently.

selection.reason: Used by EPD-0079 and philosophically sound: the nutriment link rests on the source's own rice-seedling simile.

unknowns: No participant or event has been found or confirmed. Everything here is a research direction.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. No location, scene or shot decisions are made at the idea stage.
